chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from Mu'awiyah ibn Wahb, who said:
I said to Abī 'Abdillah عليه السلام: Should I say “Āmīn” when the Imam says
“not of those who have incurred wrath, nor of those who are astray”
He said: They are the Jews and the Christians.

And he did not answer on this point; so his turning away عليه السلام from answering what the questioner asked is evidence for the reprehensibility of this expression, even if he was not able to state its reprehensibility explicitly due to taqiyyah and necessity, so he turned away from answering him altogether.

key_terms.آمِينَ: The liturgical expression “Āmīn” said after recitation.
key_terms.التَّقِيَّةِ: Dissimulation or precautionary concealment due to circumstances of danger or constraint.
key_terms.الضَّالِّينَ: Those who are astray, explained here as the Christians.
key_terms.الْإِمَامُ: The prayer leader in congregational salat (prayer).
key_terms.الْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ: Those who incurred divine wrath, explained here as the Jews.
key_terms.كَرَاهِيَةِ: Reprehensibility or disapproved status in legal context.

ai.seo_question: What does this hadith indicate about saying “Āmīn” after al-Hamd in salat (prayer)?
ai.summary: This report concerns the ruling on saying “Āmīn” after al-Hamd in salat (prayer). The Imam عليه السلام responds instead by identifying the meaning of “those who incurred wrath” and “those who went astray,” and the accompanying note indicates that his not directly answering is taken as evidence of the dislike of uttering this phrase, in a context possibly involving taqiyyah.
